idiom_name: require/autoload + Module#const_get over a naming convention
implementation_notes: Ruby's component configuration is convention over machinery: the script lists component names or require paths, the loader requires the file (or lets autoload/Zeitwerk load it at first constant access) and resolves the class with Object.const_get("My::Component"), then instantiates it - the repository is usually a Hash on a configuration object, as in Rails initializers, Rack middleware stacks and Sidekiq-style plugin wiring. remove_const can drop a constant binding, but the class object, its methods and the loaded feature stay, so Ruby has no unlinking: reconfiguration means restarting the process or replacing a worker. A full repository/lifecycle structure is justified only when components need explicit init/shutdown hooks and dependency-ordered teardown in a long-running daemon.
code_sketch:
module ComponentRegistry
  def self.link(config)
    config.fetch("components").to_h do |entry|
      require entry.fetch("require")                 # idempotent per resolved path
      klass = Object.const_get(entry.fetch("class")) # naming convention
      [entry.fetch("name"), klass.new(**entry.fetch("args", {}))]
    end
  end
end
pitfalls: require loads a file once per resolved path while load re-executes it every call; mixing them (or using load in production) redefines classes under new identities while existing instances keep the old ones, producing 'is not the same object' defects that look like lost state.

const_get resolves any constant reachable through the namespace chain (inherited constants included), so a value taken from configuration can name arbitrary constants - validate with const_defined?(name, false) against a whitelist before resolving.

Gems and their constants are process-global: remove_const can break unrelated code that still references the constant, and a loaded gem cannot be unloaded at all, which makes 'reconfiguration' a restart in any real deployment.
